newsitem.title: ITALY: Opposition leads in main Italian mayoral races.
newsitem.headline: Opposition leads in main Italian mayoral races.

text.p: The separatist Northern League party lost control of Italy's business capital Milan on Sunday in mayoral elections that put the country's main opposition alliance ahead in several key races, according to exit polls.

Milan's outgoing mayor Marco Formentini, elected in 1993 at the height of the League's popularity, trailed a poor third to opponents from the centre-right opposition Freedom Alliance and Italy's governing centre-left Olive Tree bloc, the polls said.

Industrialist Gabriele Albertini of the Freedom Alliance was ahead in Milan with 39 to 43 percent of the vote against 25 to 29 for his Olive Tree rival Aldo Fumagalli, the exit polls showed. They will enter a second round run-off on May 11.

The Freedom Alliance was also ahead in Turin, Italy's northern industrial heart, where challenger Raffaele Costa was forecast to win 39 to 43 percent of the vote to 34 to 38 for outgoing mayor Valentino Castellani of the Olive Tree.

Conducted by Abacus for broadcasters RAI and Fininvest, the polls forecast Formentini would win only 17 to 21 percent of the vote in Milan in a blow to the prestige of the Northern League and a further sign of waning support for its separatist agenda.

Milan was the biggest prize in elections for mayors and local councils in more than 1,100 towns and cities in the first big test of electoral support since Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition won last April's general election.

In four other big cities at stake, the Olive Tree was in the lead in the northeast port of Trieste and Ancona on the Adriatic coast, while the Freedom Alliance candidate was ahead in the southern city of Catanzaro with a neck-and-neck race in Reggio Calabria. All looked set to go to a second round.
Counting in the votes, for which 9.4 million voters or about one-fifth of the national electorate was eligible, was to begin on Monday morning with official results later in the day.

The Prodi government's popularity has suffered in recent months from resentment at tax hikes it has brought in to cut the budget deficit and try to squeeze Italy into the first wave of countries to join Europe's planned single currency.

It had sought to divorce Sunday's municipal polls from its own performance, clouded by a battle of wills between centrists in the coalition and the hard left Communist Refoundation party which provides Prodi with his parliamentary majority.

But the shadow of Refoundation appeared to weigh over the key mayoral battles, with the party running alone in the main contests and suggesting it could seek a high price for swinging its voters behind centre-left candidates in the second round.

Party leader Fausto Bertinotti, preparing to do battle with Prodi over planned structural reforms to the welfare state, said the exit polls showed that the Olive Tree could not win in Milan and Turin without his backing.

"In Turin and Milan the Olive Tree is trailing the Freedom Alliance simply because it did not ally with Communist Refoundation. Otherwise we would have won," Bertinotti said. "I hope the Olive Tree does not make a suicidal choice".

Olive Tree politicians said it was too early to interpret the elections but the opposition, which had billed the ballots as an opportunity for voters to oppose Prodi, said the exit polls pointed to a slap in the face for the government.
"If the exit polls are confirmed, the elections will be transformed into a referendum against Prodi," said hard-right parliamentarian Paolo Amaroli.
He said the Milan vote was also a defeat for League leader Umberto Bossi who had "sown secession and reaped a storm".
The League rose to popularity at the height of Italy's corruption scandals in the early 1990s with vociferous attacks on graft, high taxes and central government inefficiency.

Its star has waned since last April's general election, when Bossi's failure to win the balance of power in parliament was followed by a switch from federalism to a separatist agenda and the symbolic declaration of a northern "republic of Padania".
